text.en: India is the second largest producer of rice, wheat, tea, cotton, sugarcane and fruit in the world. Which crops grow where and why?

India's crops fall into four groups: food crops, cash crops, plantation crops and horticultural crops.
Rice needs about 24 degrees Celsius, 150 cm of rain and clayey loamy soil; India is the second largest producer after China, and West Bengal is first in India.
Wheat is the second food crop; Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh give more than 85 percent of it.
Jowar and bajra are millets; Maharashtra leads in jowar and Rajasthan in bajra; pulses fix nitrogen and are rotated with other crops.
Cash crops include sugarcane, cotton, jute and oilseeds; cotton is the most important cash crop, jute is led by West Bengal and Gujarat leads in oilseeds.
Plantation crops are tea, coffee, rubber and spices; Assam leads in tea, Karnataka in coffee, and Kerala in spices; rubber was first planted in Kerala in 1902.
Livestock: cattle are 37.3 percent of livestock, Uttar Pradesh has the most buffaloes, and goat is the poor man's cow.
Fisheries employ over 14 million people; India produces about 3 percent of world fish and ranks second after China; fishing is marine or inland.
Rainfall, temperature and soil decide which crop is grown where.

problem.en: Why is Assam the leading tea state and Karnataka the leading coffee state?

text.en: Tea needs high rainfall, humid climate and light shade, which Assam's hills offer.
Coffee grows in shade at 1000 to 1500 m altitude, as in the hills of Karnataka.
So climate and altitude decide plantation locations.

Cash crops: sugarcane, cotton are sold for industry
Plantation crops are grown on estates for export

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking only wheat is a food crop
